en: Preface to the *New and Extraordinary Record of the Vajra* of the Imperial Ming Dynasty The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* takes the severing of doubt and the shattering of attachments as its primary aim. Among the five hundred and seventy-seven fascicles of the Great Collection (*Mahāsaṃnipāta*), it is titled the "Chapter on Severance" (*Cchedana-parivarta*).
To examine its origins: for all beings of the four modes of birth and twelve categories, that which must be exhausted is the physical shell; yet it is not exhausted...
This is the cycle of saṃsāra. Unless one cuts off doubt and breaks through attachment, one will be born without understanding and die without rest.

Yet, unless one enters this sutra with faith, doubt will not be severed and attachment will not be broken. For this reason, the Compassionate King of Awakening [the Buddha] employed the raft metaphor to preach the Dharma;
the wise and skillful [patriarchs] opened up the bridge for its reception and maintenance. [As recorded in] Tang’s *Duàn Tàicháng Jiūyì* and Song’s...

The Great Emperor [Taizong] recorded extensively and documented fully all instances of spiritual response; he spoke exhaustively of karmic retribution. Indeed, the realm of the unseen is of the utmost gravity.

This sutra is protected by all the celestial deities: to recite, read, or explain it brings merit as vast as the sands of the Ganges; yet to harbor doubt and fail to believe incurs transgressions as massive as mountains.
Carai (Zaisheng) the Layman has no attachments in his breast; having realized that causes arise from a mind that dwells nowhere, his person is bound [to the Dharma].
Furthermore, having planted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of roots of goodness, he gathered [the fruits] during this illustrious era to continue the legacy of former renown.

His intent was primarily to manifest new principles; thus, when wonders were witnessed, there was cause for awakening. Examining what he has recorded: the account of the monk seeing the stupa demonstrates the reverence and respect accorded to ghosts and spirits;
the account of obtaining the Buddha’s longevity examines the realization and enlightenment of the school of immortals. These two categories are intermingled, yet ultimately they obstruct the spirit.

[The Buddha] delivered [this teaching]. Hold these four lines firmly; the karma of animal existence will be instantly transformed. The divine wind manifests protection through the power of the sutra, and Vajrapāṇi appears in the form of a rescuing canopy.
As for the goose that listened to the sutra, the hen that incubated her eggs, and the spider that shed its skin—they were neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings.
Wu You traveled to the netherworld; Wang Hui returned to life. Shi completed the sutras. This "single unified mark" is not a single unified mark.

Nianfo attained the vast clarity that reaches heaven and wandered by seizing other bodies. The woman who wove sutras and passed away while seated—Jixiang Shanshi—copied sutras in a dark room, radiating the constant light of compassion and wisdom.
She exhorted her kin to listen to the sutras, manifesting the ultimate filiality of providing support. [She] petitioned...
The Master cleansed the habitual minds of the fishermen; the elderly neighbor and the military official were moved by his spiritual wonders.
The monastery invited him, and he chanted as a medium for the immortals, demonstrating that among all human merits, this is the most supreme. Is it not so?

Like the blind man regaining his son and the servant extending his years, one perceives the extinction of the karmic offenses of previous lives. Truly, the realization of Bodhi is like the fragrance of jade produced when summer passes.
Preface to the *New and Extraordinary Record of the Vajra of the Imperial Ming*:
Within the great mass of raging fire, not a single thing can remain; yet that which cannot be destroyed is the vajra.
The vajra is produced from within refined gold and resembles purple quartz; its color is like wheat bran. Its hardness and sharpness are such that it can destroy all things. And yet—
Nothing can destroy it; therefore, it is called "vajra. It is the hardest among metals, not merely worldly hardness.
My wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind is able to shatter the six sense-objects while remaining as-it-is and unmoving; this analogy is the most apt of all.
Thus, the Great Hero (the Buddha) is not even a hair’s breadth different from those of the four modes of birth and the twelve classes of beings.

Therefore, they converge within the state of suchness (*tathatā*), which is immovable. Since this is the reality, it is the ultimate intent; when the single breath moves, cause and effect do not fail. Who could then dismiss them as non-existent?

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the very marrow of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; its recitation and upholding have been most flourishing in China, and it has consequently been widely published throughout the world.
The karmic retributions for attaining the fruit of the Vajra [Vehicle] are generally derived from various records of marvels and anomalies (*guoyi*).
These are detailed in the Tang and Song dynasties but sparse in our Ming dynasty. I maintain that when ordinary people become complacent regarding long-established traditions, they grow negligent;

negligence gives rise to an evil mind. Conversely, novelty and strangeness cause one to be alert; alertness gives rise to a virtuous mind. The events of antiquity have already been recorded, yet the heavens of this late age...
Approaching gradually, the doctrine of cause and effect is not a matter of a hundred years, nor of several decades, nor even seven or eight years, nor five or six years.
It is not easy to persuade those who have merely heard of it or witnessed it with their own eyes—those who use the *Pāyāsi Sutta* as a pretext and treat the common talk of the elderly with disdain.
This must be transformed and shifted. I have searched through my miscellaneous records of ordinary times; all of these are from the scriptures.
I have compiled the various accounts of miraculous responses—those that constitute the greater portion of this work—as well as other matters I have heard from the elders of my village.
Having read through these compilations repeatedly, my hair stands on end and sweat flows; they are all, indeed, like Tian Dan amidst the flames.
This is not the work of Tian Dan, who wore golden girdles across his waist. It is a compilation of what exists in other lands and what has been recorded by others;

there must surely be things far more manifest and striking than these, a hundredfold or even a thousandfold greater. May those gentlemen who are skilled in propagation ensure that these accounts do not perish, but rather spread them skillfully.
I look with earnest hope to such virtuous men who act for the good of others. Therefore, it is entitled *The New and Extraordinary Record of the Golden Mantra of the August Brilliance*.
Preface by the Layman Wang Qilong of Xiushui.
Following the Preface by Prince [Wang Zhen], a critic says:
"The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the most supreme of the Prajñā teachings; why do you, sir, extensively compile records of cause and effect?"
"Is it then that one seeks Bodhi by grasping at signs? He replied, "There are three types of people who uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The first type is like the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch: while carrying firewood through the marketplace, upon hearing the phrase 'no-mind arising,' he suddenly received the seal of the patriarchs.
When Zen Master Zhongfeng reached the passage on *Samyak-saṃbodhi*, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment throughout the entire sūtra—what is called 'not [remaining] after a single word.'"
It cannot be grasped through deliberation or conjecture; it is precisely this "entirety of Prajñā" that one carries upon one's shoulders.

As for those of the second grade, they read and understand the meaning, investigating and seeking with precision. Regarding the principle of "relying on the meaning and not on the words," this refers to having a distinct realization beneath the words, whereby the entirety of Prajñā is gradually sealed within them.
As for those of the third grade, they merely recite following the sounds of the text.
One relies solely upon this to achieve spiritual resonance and miraculous response, to resist and disperse distraction, and to spur on the dull and stubborn.
This is what is meant by "awakening and inspiration arising from words," whereby one receives and practices with faith the Prajñāpāramitā that pervades the entire body through various skillful means.
In the final age of the Buddha-dharma, those of the first rank are as rare as the udumbara flower, seldom seen in the world; those of the second rank are like the [blue lotus]...
The lotus and vermilion grass are likewise rare encounters; only those of the third grade are like common timber and ordinary flora, filling the eyes everywhere.
If such people do not seek Bodhi while clinging to signs, would they not at least create karma while clinging to signs?
This compilation is intended solely to preach the Dharma for those of the third grade, not for the first or second. The Buddha’s words were given according to the illness.
Administering the medicine: from the outset, there is no fixed attachment. Speaking of the present, since originally there has been no thing, where could dust be provoked?

Regarding Prajñā, it merely fosters wild wisdom. If one sweeps and wipes away [delusions] at all times so that dust does not settle, then Prajñā will become a blade thrust into the chest and a needle inserted into the crown of the head;
like drilling wood to produce fire, the light will manifest throughout the entire body. Read the *Golden* well.

A person who has just begun their study of the sutras must certainly not exchange that for this. Wang Mohe said: "The Dharma transcends verbal expression; one who fully understands verbal expression is liberated.
Thus, one may speak all day long. "The Dharma is without name or mark; one who knows name and mark is True Suchness. Thus, one may speak all day long.
When has there ever been a destruction of marks? Excellent indeed are these few words; they penetrate to the ultimate essentials of Prajñā.
I venture to present them openly upon the tray, lest wild Chan practitioners lightly hand over such a sharp instrument to those who treat it as mere worthless chaff.
This preface was written by the lay practitioner Dai Sheng Wang Qilong of Xiushui.

The *New and Extraordinary Record of the Vajra [Teachings] of the Imperial Ming*,
compiled by the Layman Cai-sheng of Xiushui, Wang Qilong;

During the Hongzhi era, the Zhenru Pagoda in Hejun of Jusi Prefecture had collapsed and was undergoing extensive reconstruction.

At that time, there was a dhūta practitioner named Huailin who, for over twenty years, solicited donations while dragging a three-zhang-long iron chain. Once the pagoda construction was completed, he immediately turned his head back toward...

In the stupa, his portrait is enshrined for worship today. Tradition holds that when this *dhūta* practitioner was first a monk at Chengtian Temple in Suzhou, he drank wine, consumed meat, and held the precepts in contempt.
While seeking coolness on a summer day, he suddenly beheld two infernal executioners entering and binding him by the neck;
they were leading about ten people in fetters, and the *dhūta*’s name was also listed among them. He devised a plan to bribe the two executioners.
He prepared several paper ingots and flowers. He delayed the departure for seven days, intending to wait for others from Qi to join him.
The two soldiers joyfully granted his request. The dhūta wept as he informed his disciples; they purchased paper ingots and burned them, carrying out his instructions until everything was finished.
Someone informed him that Chan Master Ru of Zhēnrú had attained a high level of spiritual practice. "Traveling by boat for the distance of one day's journey, why not go there to seek him?
The Tóuduó followed these words and came. He wept bitterly and made his plea. The Chan Master said, "The stupa here is about to collapse.
If you are willing to exert your sincerity and resolve to solicit donations for its restoration, I shall transmit the Dharma-gate to you and guarantee that ghosts will be unable to constrain you."
[The monk] heard this. The dhūta practitioner immediately made a vow before the Buddha. The Chan Master took a rosary in his hand and gave it to him, saying, "Do not sleep for seven days;
simply stay in my room and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. You should know that this very place shall become a stūpa."

Two lines were sufficient. Dharma Master Touduo recited them as instructed for over seven months. One night, two shadowy soldiers arrived at the Master’s quarters, stumbling and prostrating themselves on the ground, pleading:
"There is a monk who ought to die who has fled to this place; we beg you to instruct us on the means to apprehend him.
The Master said, "He is in his room; you may seize him as you please. Why ask me? The two soldiers entered, but immediately came out in a state of alarm, saying, "The room—"
He stopped and saw a jeweled stupa, its brilliant radiance so intense that his eyes watered and he could not open them even slightly.
The Chan Master said, "Because he recites the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle and has made courageous, great vows, even devas, nāgas, and spirits can do nothing against him."
"You need only reply to the Lord of the Netherworld: 'A certain monk, a certain master, has retained this for the repair of a stupa.
Since the merit of both the hidden and the manifest worlds shall be shared, you will certainly not suffer for this grave offense. The two soldiers, having no other choice, bowed weeping and departed.

The dhūta then forged these iron chains to bind himself, dragging them along the roads; he did not shrink from the distance of the journey through the intense cold of winter or the scorching heat of summer, seeking out those of virtue.
I believe that he was ultimately able to complete this great merit with the remaining years of his life. As the Sūtra says:
"The obstructing Māra searched for a thousand years without finding the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha. Consider this practice of the dhūta of stūpa-building.
Is this not indeed so? During the Zhengde era of the Ming dynasty,
when the Buddha’s longevity was attained,
the Daoist Chen Xuan of Heming Guan in Western Sichuan sought longevity with resolute intent, contemplating it day and night.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a deity whose appearance was extraordinary. Calling himself the Vajrapāṇi Deity, he told Huixuan:
"If you seek long life, go quickly to Mount Min to pay homage to Master Zhirong; he shall transmit to you the Dharma of longevity.

Huixuan acted according to these words and earnestly requested instruction. Zhirong said: "The verses of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* state: 'All conditioned phenomena are like a dream...'"
"Like a phantom, a bubble, a shadow; like dew, and also like lightning—thus should one contemplate. This was my Buddha’s teaching on longevity.
Huizang asked, "If it is like an illusion or a dream, what is meant by 'longevity'? Daorong shouted, "All marks are non-marks;
the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi* does not enter into annihilation. At these words, Huizang attained great enlightenment and subsequently took his leave to live in seclusion at Wagushan.

He lived on the southern slope of Huju Rock; he did not cease his profound meditative absorption and daily recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until he had completed several entire collections (piṭakas).
He reached the age of ninety-eight. One day, he gathered all the recluses living nearby and said to them, "In the beginning, I sought the immortality of the transcendents (xian);
now, I have finally attained the Buddha’s immortality. I hope that you gentlemen may obtain what I have obtained. Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes.

He passed away. Several hundred families near Wawushan built a shrine together to enshrine his portrait and worship him as Xuán, asserting that he had attained both the Way of the Immortals and the Fruit of the Buddhas.
Xu Guān of Zhāo served as the Governor of Sichuan and personally recorded these events.

During the Zhengde era, when this sutra was being upheld for longevity, there was a great virtuous monk on Mount Nanyue named Chushi. He was widely versed in the Tripitaka and specialized in the recitation of the Diamond Sutra.
Whenever anyone paid their respects to him or requested the Buddha-dharma—whether they were wise or foolish, noble or lowly—he would immediately call out in a loud voice, "Excellent! (Hao!).
He took the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with him and passed away at the age of one hundred and seventy-one.
At that same time, there were the monks Baiting and Wuji, who also specialized in exhorting others to practice and uphold the *Vajracchedikā*.

Baiting reached the age of one hundred and thirty, and Wuji reached the age of one hundred and twenty-four. By praying for longevity, they obtained longevity; by praying for Great Nirvāṇa, they attained it.
"Attaining Great Nirvana—how could this be empty talk? Yan Jiang attained transformation at the foot of a tree by the river.
He was a leather-worker from Xiangcheng who, in his middle years, abandoned his trade to carry offerings of rice and food to Buddhist temples. On the road, he focused exclusively on...

He maintained the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the name of Amitābha Buddha without ceasing his voice. At over sixty years of age, he suddenly ceased eating grain and subsisted on water for one month.
He then declared, "I shall depart on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such a time.

When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Upon cremation, several *he* (measures) of *śarīra* relics were obtained; his tongue remained as firm as metal or stone.
When tapped, it produces a sound. This event took place in the thirteenth year of the Zhengde era and is recorded in the Xiangcheng Gazetteer.
I have transcribed this here to inform those who sincerely uphold the sutras and recite the Buddha’s name.
Regarding the two characters "intermingled" (*jiázá*):
when the Vice Commander-in-Chief Nan-tang Qi Gong was serving as a Deputy Commander-in-Chief, he led troops to defend the Three Rivers during the Japanese incursions.

The General had long been devoutly devoted to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and did not cease his recitation even while in the midst of military operations. One night, he dreamed of a certain soldier who had perished in battle.
He requested that one scroll of a sutra be recited to provide for his liberation. On the following morning, the soldier’s wife came to report that her dream was exactly as described.
The official rose at dawn, observed the fast, and recited the scripture with single-minded devotion. That evening, the soldier’s wife dreamed that her husband spoke to her, saying:

"I am grateful that my master has recited the sutra for me; however, because the text was interspersed with the two characters 'bu' (not) and 'yong' (use), the merit is incomplete, and I have not yet attained [liberation]."

She was merely freed from suffering. On the following morning, the soldier’s wife again appealed to him with a dream. The Duke was greatly surprised; he then recalled that while he was reciting the sutra, a maidservant brought tea and cakes to him.
He had waved his hand to dismiss her; though he had not spoken, his intention had been to say they were not needed.
The Duke once spoke of this matter to his attendants, and the story subsequently spread. Alas! If even a single thought is tainted by impurity, the unseen realm knows it immediately.
Can those who recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* truly increase their karmic burden for the hungry ghosts by reciting it with a distracted mind, merely following along with their lips?
Feng Qin Yan’nan (Feng Qin).

A person of the Jiajing era, he was a domestic servant in the household of Mao Lumen of Guian. An astrologer predicted his impending misfortune and asked an elderly monk how he might extend his years.
The old monk said, "As a servant, you lack the power to accumulate merit; you can only... [sprinkle water...]
He collected discarded paper and recited the Diamond Sūtra, hoping thereby to avoid an untimely death. He then procured a pair of bamboo tweezers and a bamboo basket;
during the day, he traversed the village lanes, plucking every piece of defiled or discarded paper into the basket with the tweezers, which he then purified with scented water.
She dried [the remains] in the sun, burned them to ash, and sent them wrapped away in a clear stream. She never neglected even a single character [of scripture].

When returning home at night, she would kneel and recite one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as a dedication of merit; this became her constant practice for years. Later, she gradually learned to read and understood the meaning of the texts, and Lu-men also treated her with courtesy.
Her household became prosperous and well-off; she had two sons and four grandsons. At the age of ninety-five, she passed away without illness.
The Divine Wind Obtains the Scripture:
At a certain temple on Mount Dongting, there was a complete scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written by the Tang dynasty poet Bai Juyi.

It served as the temple’s most precious treasure. In the forty-third year of the Jiajing era, a famine struck the southeast; the monks were starving, and the presiding monk used the scripture as collateral for a loan.

The official Wang Huan had provided fifty *shí* of rice from Mount Tang for his sustenance. After a year had passed, Wang Huan summoned the presiding monk to his home and expressed his wish to donate the aforementioned rice for the purpose of providing a vegetarian feast for the monastics;
he then returned the scriptures to him. As the monk was returning and crossing the lake, he praised the virtue of the official before the assembly.
The members of the boat all requested to see the scriptures once more. When they were unfurled, a great wind arose from the heavens, and the scriptures were ultimately revealed.
The preceding several fascicles drifted into the air and vanished into the clouds. The monk was filled with unremitting regret and returned the scripture to its original place in the temple.
Three years later, a certain unworthy official heard the name of this scripture and had the presiding monk arrested on some other pretext.
He was detained and forced to offer it up. When the scripture arrived, because it was incomplete and did not satisfy his wishes, he returned it to the monk Seng.
As the monk returned to his boat, a great storm arose again; in the pitch-black darkness, the boat entered a deep village to seek shelter from the wind.
Having disembarked to seek fire, he went to the house of an elderly fisherman, where several scrolls of the aforementioned scripture were found stuck to the wall, completely undamaged.
The fisherman was surnamed Yao and was illiterate. When questioned, he merely said that three years prior, a streak of fire had fallen into his field;
startled, he looked at it and saw it was paper with characters written upon it. Finding this strange, he pasted it onto the wall.

The monk gazed at the several scrolls with tears of sorrow and prostrated himself, calling incessantly upon the Dharma-protecting deity Vajrapāṇi, saying: "Were it not for the two successive divine winds manifesting this marvel, this scripture..."

He was detained by powerful officials and could not return to restore the scriptures at Hepu. Consequently, he recounted the entire sequence of events to a fisherman, who was deeply moved and struck with wonder.
The fisherman subsequently changed his occupation to farming and provided the funds to re-enshrine these scriptures.

Every year on the anniversary of the scriptures' return, he would invariably go to the temple to pay his respects. He lived to the age of eighty-two and passed away peacefully without illness. Alas! This...

Is it not even more miraculous that a snail traveled a thousand li to return with the scripture? Regarding the seven characters of the scripture’s title: in the Jisi year of the Longqing era, the wife of Wang De-yong, a retired scholar from Tianle Township in Shaoxing, became ill one day. Wang De-yong was a lay practitioner of the Tiantai school who had long been devoted to the Lotus Sutra. His wife, née Tao, was also a devout follower of the Dharma. One day, she fell ill; her condition grew increasingly grave, and she could not eat or drink. Her husband, De-yong, wept as he attended to her. He then took the Lotus Sutra and placed it upon his wife’s head. Suddenly, she felt a sensation as if something were being inserted into her mouth. She immediately opened her eyes and spoke, saying, "I am now well. She then sat up and requested a copy of the scripture. De-yong gave it to her, and she read it herself. After reading it once, she said, "I have already received this scripture in a previous life. She then recited the scripture’s title from memory: "The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma. Having finished speaking, she passed away peacefully. De-yong buried her according to the rites. Later, while digging the grave, they discovered a small snail shell within her coffin. It was about two inches long and one inch wide. Inside the shell was a piece of paper, folded and rolled, upon which the aforementioned seven characters of the scripture’s title were written in ink. De-yong presented this to the authorities. The local officials were astonished and reported it to the provincial governor. The governor issued an edict proclaiming the event throughout the prefecture. This account is recorded in the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), fascicle 49, and the *Shishi Yaolan* (Essentials of Buddhist History), fascicle 20. It is truly a rare and extraordinary occurrence. Furthermore, there is the case of the monk Huiming of Mount Lu, who recovered from illness by reciting the *Heart Sutra*. These instances demonstrate that the power of the Buddha-Dharma is unfathomable and its efficacy is manifest. May all those who encounter these accounts take them to heart and practice accordingly. Do not doubt the truth of these matters. Thus ends this brief record. May it serve as a cause for the eradication of suffering and the attainment of liberation for all beings. Du heard two ghost messengers say, "Your allotted years have already expired. Furthermore, throughout your life you have performed no virtuous deeds;
you shall surely fall into the evil realms. In an instant, he indeed beheld the terrifying manifestations of hell. He said to his husband, "Hell has appeared before us; how can we save me?
Suddenly, he remembered that the Elder Duan of the neighboring temple recited the sutras every day, and because he had once memorized the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, [he began to recite it].
She recited the seven characters of the *Pāramitā* with extreme vigor and intensity for several thousand times. The hell that had previously appeared before her then vanished from sight.
Suddenly, the family members attending to her illness saw five-colored light emanating from Tao’s mouth.
From the air came a faint voice saying, "The virtuous woman Tao has already escaped falling into hell and has been reborn in a good realm. The entire village was moved.
Everyone transmitted this account. By reciting the seven characters of the scripture’s title, one may escape the depths of samsara. This was recorded by the layman Bao Xingquan.

When the Second Patriarch returned to Qiantang by imperial decree, Li Shiying was serving as the Magistrate of Qin Prefecture in Nanhai. He had long been a reciter of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In the Dingmao year of the Longqing era...

While serving as an examination proctor, he died of illness within the examination hall after three days. Initially, he saw a deity in golden armor who intended to take him away to see the Lord of Mount Tai;
however, the City God and the Local Deity were all present, and because Li Song had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, [the deity was deterred].
Sengjian refused to sign his name. The deity in golden armor grew enraged; drawing a fire-nail over three feet long from his sleeve, he drove it through the crown of the Local Deity’s head.
Immediately, the deity was seen to be completely consumed by flames. In an instant, the deity returned to his original form. Sengjian remained obstinate and continued as before not to sign.
The deity in golden armor said, "I shall lock you up together and send you to Mount Tai. The Local Deity replied, "As for seeing Mount Tai, I have my own memorial to submit."

Suddenly, several ghosts appeared, crying out in grievance and demanding his life. Shi Ying realized that in a previous life he had served as the Governor of Jiujiang and had accepted bribes to kill people.
In the midst of his intense panic, he recalled and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Suddenly, Master Lü descended upon the clouds. The ghosts all fled in haste.
Shi Ying prostrated himself on the ground and begged for mercy. Master Lü said, "Return to me the elixir of the Old Lord. He looked closely once more.

He said, "Karmic retribution! Karmic retribution! It is a pity that all the cinnabar has been utterly destroyed. You recited the *Vajracchedikā*, which can be used to seek salvation from the Sixth Patriarch.

Suddenly, the Sixth Patriarch arrived. Upon seeing him, Daoying prostrated himself on the ground and also cried out, "Karmic retribution! Karmic retribution! I have come to deliberate with you, the Fifth Patriarch.
Daoying reached out a hand and pulled at the Sixth Patriarch’s cassock; it came apart piece by piece, scattering like gold.
It was light. After a short while, suddenly a wondrous fragrance filled his nostrils. He heard the Fifth and Sixth Patriarchs from the air commanding:

"Let the person who recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* go back for now. Immediately, he saw the previously mentioned god in golden armor arrive again, seize Shi Ying, and hurl him away with a single toss.
Sweat poured from him like rain and he revived. At that time, Daoying left the monastic order and retired to Jingci Temple in Hunan to practice ascetic cultivation.
Every morning he would invariably recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to deliver the spirits of the deceased from their grievances. Later, he passed away without illness.
The śramaṇa Guangche:
In the city of Hangzhou, there was a wild monk named Guangche, who styled himself "Tongtian" (Penetrating the Heavens).

He begged from the Vice-Minister Jin Shengwu for a pure site where he might recite the sutras and practice nianfo. Minister Zhang Yuanzhou possessed a family shrine named Zifu, which was quite pure; [Shengwu] [requested it].
He obtained it from a beggar. During the day, Guangche recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; at night, he carried a lantern and circumambulated the streets chanting the Buddha’s name.
One evening, while Xingwu was seeing off a guest, he encountered him. He wrote upon the man’s lantern: "The Śramaṇa Guangche chants the Buddha’s name; his devotion penetrates the heavens.
On a certain month and day, Guangche passed away while facing the image in the temple. [This was reported by] a Prince of [Place Name] in Huguang.
That evening, he dreamed of a monk who burst into the palace and said, "I am a monk from Zifu Temple in Hangzhou, come to serve as a prince.

When the King looked at the monk’s hand, which held a basket, eight characters were clearly visible within it. Startled, he awoke; the inner palace had already reported that a crown prince had been born.
The King specially dispatched an officer to Hangzhou to investigate the matter, discovering that the night the monk passed away was precisely the night of the King's dream.

At that time, was it perhaps because his causes for merit were so profound and weighty that he left his body to travel elsewhere? How could the doctrine of cause and effect be called a mere fabrication?
This occurred during the early years of the Wanli era.

Xianhou Zheng’s mother, Sheng Zai-de of Fengqiao in Suzhou, received the scriptures from the lecturer Xuanming. At the beginning of the Wanli era, she fell ill and went before the Office of the Netherworld.
There, she was summoned for interrogation by the transformed spirit of her enemy, Sheng. Because Zai-de’s case was just, she was released.
When Guanming returned from the underworld, his vision ceased for the night. The next day, he saw the Governor descend the steps of the rampart and address him, saying:
"In my previous life, I was a man of Jingzhou surnamed Cao. Since I ascended to the Divine Registers, my mother, Lady Zhang, has been reborn three times, each time as a woman who failed to conceive.

If you would act on my behalf and earnestly entreat a master of profound insight to reverently recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Candrottarādārikāparipṛcchā Sūtra*, [she may be liberated]."
Each [copy] was in five hundred fascicles. He rescued his mother by transforming her into a male; his exhortations were most earnest. She was reborn through his virtue.

He respectfully requested Xuanming to chant the full text of the petition and announce it. Master Guandongming composed a preface to record this, which is contained in the *Xutiji* (Continued Collection) of Cai Ti.
Wanhu Zi was born at the beginning of the Wanli era. A certain Wanhu in Wuzhong had no son for many years despite his prayers and supplications.

He sought counsel from an elderly Chan master, who said, "Not yet. You already have a son, though he is a practitioner of the Way. He is currently prostrating and reciting the *Golden [Light Sutra] at such-and-such a place."*

He had recited one entire collection (*piṭaka*) of the *Diamond Sūtra* and was raising funds to repair a road; it was calculated that its completion would still require three years before he could finally take rebirth.
The Myriarch dispatched men to search for him, and indeed, after three years, when the sūtras were finished and the road construction completed, the practitioner died and the Myriarch’s son was born.
Upon inquiry, it was found that the dates of their deaths and births coincided exactly. Thus, one knows that while living...
The gilded lion throne was draped with brocade; this was indeed a matter of great merit for humans and devas, not a trivial affair.
In the early years of the Wanli era, Zhong Gongfuxiu and Xu Gongzunsou, both serving as Grand Secretaries, resided together in Luojia Lane and devoted themselves to the Buddha.

They maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. They separately prepared a pure Buddha-chamber where the two masters sat side by side to recite it. The master of the bell had two white geese;
whenever they heard the sutra or the chanting of the Buddha's name, the geese would follow behind the two masters, making sounds as they went. Even when chased away, they would not leave.
They did not draw near to harass him; whether walking or standing still, they followed the sound of the wooden fish drum.

During the severe cold, their webbed feet were frozen and cracked, yet they walked with exposed bones, exerting even greater effort. After several years, both geese stood facing the sutra table and passed away together.
The two masters buried them on the grounds behind Jingye Temple, naming the site "The Tomb of the Geese Who Listened to the Sutras."
Among the salt-fishermen were Zhang Yuan and his younger brother Zhang Zhen. One night, as they returned from casting their nets, their boat reached Qingsong Tang.
They saw an extraordinary light upon the water’s surface that eclipsed the stars and moon; suspecting there might be oyster pearls beneath, they dove to retrieve it and found a stone.
There was a single casket. The brothers congratulated one another; they returned home, prayed, and only then opened it.

Inside, they found one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, written in golden characters, its brilliance extraordinary. Originally, it had been quite plain, and they had simply kept it in their household.
In the middle of the night, he dreamed that a deity clad in golden armor spoke to him, saying: "In a previous life, you were a laborer at the lecture hall of Dharma Master Changshui.
Because your resolve for the Way was not firm, you fell back and descended to this state. Nevertheless, your past causes have not perished; I shall bestow upon you the Great Dharma."
One should diligently maintain the recitation. Originally, Yuan used his illiteracy as an excuse;

however, a deity caused his mouth to open and cast a golden pill into it, which was brilliant with light and entered his belly with a warm fragrance. He then started awake in surprise. The next day, when he began his recitation, it was as proficient as if he had practiced for a long time.
Yuan went to consult Master Daguan and related the matter in detail. The Master further encouraged him, saying that one must certainly recite the sutras.

He dedicated his merit toward rebirth in the Western Paradise. Three years later, Yuan said to his relatives and acquaintances, "My karmic burden of killing has been cleared away; the lotus pedestal has appeared.
Without illness, he sat upright and passed away. This occurred during the first month of autumn in the Dingchou year of the Wanli era.

When Mr. Wang Fanglu of Jintan was seriously ill and experiencing agitation, his son Sun’an approached him and said: "Father, you have cultivated yourself through constant refinement during your daily life;
this is precisely the moment for such cultivation to be fully realized. Would it not be well if you were to settle your mind and listen as your son recites the sutras?"
Fanglu nodded his head and chin in understanding. He instructed Sun’an to take up the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and recite it aloud.

When they reached the four lines beginning with "no mark of self" and "no mark of person," Fanglu suddenly laughed and said, "Afflictions are fundamentally non-existent; who would cling to a mark of self? Thereupon, he joined his palms and passed away.
Because Fanglu had obtained the hand of the Master, he turned at a single stroke; yet Sun’an was able to provide such exhortation even as his own master was on the verge of death.
Listening to the sutras in person is truly an act of filial piety in sending off the deceased that far surpasses ordinary sentiments by ten or a hundredfold.

Mr. Shen Guanghua of Jiahe, who once served as the Commissioner for Salt and Iron in the two Huai regions, happened to be with a fellow native from the same commandery on the day he retired to his estate. When he was about to receive the sutra...
He was sitting idly with Mr. Wu Song when they relaxed and took turns asking one another what they had been doing during the day.

Shen said, "In the mornings I have maintained a vegetarian diet and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for twenty years; I have already mastered the two collections [of the Tripitaka]. Mr. Wu merely set this aside with indifference. Not long after, Mr.
Wu suddenly rose at dawn and hurried to see Shen to offer congratulations, saying, "If you take the Southern Provincial Examination, you will certainly pass. Shen—

Question: Why was this? It is said that in a dream, a person told him: "A scholar in the district has obtained a high degree for his son by virtue of his merit from upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Upon waking, he remembered only that you, sir, should fulfill this dream. That autumn, Shen Gong Shuzi passed the provincial examination for the Imperial University;
it was indeed confirmed that Shen Gong had been most devout in his recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. And...

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he was able to recite [the scriptures] from memory. Once, while traveling back and forth on the road from the home of Jizi of the Eastern Ward, he maintained his recitation with single-minded concentration.
It is impossible to calculate how many people who passed through butcher shops, marketplaces, or the open air were touched by the merit of these scriptures and thereby attained transcendence.
Furthermore, he cultivated all wholesome dharmas with a mind free from the four marks [of self, person, being, and life], accumulating merit over successive lifetimes.

...virtue. Consequently, his descendants have maintained a continuous succession of success in the imperial examinations, becoming the preeminent clan of Hezhou. This is all recorded as a verification of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*.

For instance, there was a resident of Kunshan County named Zou Gui, who sold fermented bean curd for a living and was originally illiterate. One day, he heard a monk reciting the *Jin*... [text truncated]
He was reciting the Diamond Sūtra when he heard the sound of a cart stopping nearby. He remembered only four lines:
"no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, no mark of life-span. He held these firmly in mind. On the tenth day of the tenth month in the eleventh year of the Wanli era, he died.
He was escorted by infernal soldiers to the cattle pen of Li Zuofang’s house in Suzhou, where he saw others who had arrived there before him.
Two men appeared, and the infernal officer said, "Your allotted years in the world have ended; by order of the Lord of the Underworld, you are to be judged for a rebirth here for thirteen years.

Daogui realized he was about to enter an ox's womb, so he simply held fast to the four lines of verse without ceasing. The infernal officer exerted all his strength to push Daogui, but could not come near him.
Suddenly, a voice was heard saying, "Those four lines are in his heart; let him go back for now so that he may complete his recitation."
The sutra was intended as an exhortation for those who recite it in the world of the living; thus, the ritual was successfully performed and the story spread.
A neighbor went to Li’s workshop at the Chang Gate to inquire, and he learned that on the night of that very day, a cow had given birth to three calves, one of whom died.
Daogui was struck with awe and moved by emotion; he entered the monastic order to take [the master] as his teacher. He was instructed in the entire scripture and recited it day and night.

After more than thirteen years, he passed away at home without illness. Alas! Had it not been for these four lines of the scripture, Daogui’s remaining life would have been spent entirely as days of dragging plows and bearing heavy burdens.
That he died at the appointed time without illness and was reborn in a blessed realm—of this, what need is there to speak? (Jin)
It is truly the case that the numinous power of the *Vajracchedikā* can transform fixed karma.
In the Gengyin year of the Wanli era, an old man in Hualin Town, Huzhou, who recited the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* as his daily practice, was delivered from a domestic hen.
In that household, there was a hen incubating twelve eggs.

One night, the old man had a dream in which twelve boys and girls bowed before him in the hall and said, "We owe our deliverance from the realm of birds entirely to the sound of your recitation; therefore, we have come to express our gratitude.

Upon waking, the old man happened to think of the twelve chicken eggs. He took them out and found them to be remarkably light. When he split them open to look, they were merely empty shells. Thereupon, he called together the assembly.
The transmission was examined; when it was split open, both were found to be exactly as described. One must believe that the merit of upholding this sūtra is truly inconceivable.
Jin-gang Zhengfu, a resident of Zhaoli Bridge in Jiaxing who runs a green fruit shop named Kaicheng, always recites the *Jin-gang* [Sūtra] every morning upon rising.
He carried the *Diamond Sūtra* with him; whenever he went abroad, he would store the scripture in a silk pouch and suspend it at his chest, never neglecting its recitation.
In the winter of the *wanshi* year *Guisi* (1613), he traveled to Mount Dongting to sell tangerines. Midway across the great lake, he was suddenly struck by a dragon-wind.

The surface of the lake turned pitch black, and his boat was tossed about like a leaf. He lost all oars and paddles, and massive waves rose as high as houses, towering a full ten feet above the vessel.
The rest had already sunk to the bottom of the water. Amidst their cries for help, suddenly as if by some great power, the boat was lifted up and pulled out from amidst the waves;
it was carried along as if flying, reaching the mouth of Wengjiazui and landing on shore in an instant.
Then, those on the shore all saw two deities in golden armor moving through the water, carrying the boat on either side as they approached. The people on the boat knew this to be...
Vajra rescued them from drowning; they collectively felt his virtue for saving them from submersion and named him the "Blue Fruit Buddha Who Saves from Drowning.
His fame spread far and wide, and litigants requested his scriptures.
In the village lived the lay practitioner Moqing Hong. While at the Lengyan Sutra lecture hall, he encountered a man from Changzhou who was requesting a copy of the sutra;
the man was muttering the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* under his breath. Observing his countenance, it appeared truly terrifying.

Moqing asked him, "For what karmic reason are you reciting the sutra while on the road? The man replied, "I was skilled with the brush and pen and served as a litigant for a long time. One day I died of illness."
Upon arriving before King Yama, my past transgressions and evils were investigated. I presented my defense, claiming I was not guilty.

The King commanded the wardens to bring the aggrieved parties, such-and-such individuals, to testify, saying: "Are these people truly as you claim—reduced to the brink of death by your false accusations?"

I had no way to defend myself or excuse my actions, so I raised my voice and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King stood up solemnly; seeing him rise, I continued to chant with increasing fervor.
The King immediately ordered that I be released for now. [The executioner] So-and-so cried out, "This man has suffered injustice for several years and has had no means to seek retribution.
Now that he has arrived here today, you must by no means let him go. The King said, "His yang-number is still—"
I did not seize him because of his evil; he continued to recite the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle (Anuttara-yāna) in a loud voice.

I was at a loss for what to do and merely released him, allowing him to exhaust his allotted lifespan. He is an evil man; even after leaving, he will surely continue as before to commit evil and refuse to recite the scriptures.
It will not be too late for me to pursue and capture him when he stops reciting the scriptures. By these causes and conditions, he was reborn again.
In this world of the living, I have therefore changed my conduct to follow what is good, fearing that karmic retribution might eventually meet me.

Thus, I recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily and dedicate the merit toward their deliverance, hoping thereby to dissolve [the karmic debt]. Recorded on a clear day in the ninth month of autumn in the Gengzi year of the Wanli era. By Qin Hong.

In the *wàn-lì* year of *xīnchǒu* (1581), during the reign of the Sage King (Shànshì), Zhang Ai, an eunuch of the Shùn Gate Palace, devoted himself to the recitation and upholding of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in his later years.

When he reached the point where he was about to change his bedding (i.e., when death was imminent), his family members exhorted him, saying, "Do not forget the intention of upholding the sutra. Zhang Ai agreed to this, yet his mouth remained closed and he could not speak.

He was able to answer. Two green-clad attendants saw him and pressed him, saying, "You must go to the east of the mountains to take rebirth. His movement was like flying, and within a month he had already arrived in the eastern region.
There he beheld the mountains and waters of that land, as well as his parents who were to be his future birth-givers;

he loved them with single-minded devotion and focused solely on upholding the sutras. As they escorted him to a palace hall, he suspected it was the Temple of the Eastern Peak (Mount Tai), yet there were no ox-headed jailers present. The hall...
The first person wore a flat-topped crown and led the "Craving" forward. The wearer of the crown rose and said, "You ought to reach this place to enter a womb.
Craving replied, "In my life, I have upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. I only wish to be reborn in the Pure Land; I do not wish to enter a womb.

The wearer of the crown said, "Your merit from upholding the sūtra is slight. Craving said, "I have heard that even ten recitations can achieve success; how much more so for one who has upheld the sūtra?"
After many years had passed, the elder looked back at his two attendants in green and said, "Return the scripture-holder for now.

Although he has been dead for nine days, his heart is still warm; he has not yet been encoffined and will revive. He then left his home and went to Bichun Temple on the Western Mountain, where he devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
After eleven more years, one day he gathered the assembly and said, "By the power of my recitation of this scripture, today—"
He passed away facing west. Having bathed and changed his robes, he sat upright and departed this life.
An elderly neighbor brought a scripture back to Mao Feng Gong Xinghai; his courtesy name was Yigao. His eldest son was Guanglu Qing Wuzhi Gong; his courtesy name was Rui.
He was summoned and appointed as a distinguished scholar to enter the National University (Seongjun). Before he had passed the examinations, there was an elderly neighbor who lived in a thatched hut.

He observed the fasts and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Being poor and childless, on the first day of the New Year in the year of Dingyou, while he was in the midst of reciting the sutra, he suddenly saw Vajrapāṇi—clad in golden armor and holding a mace—descend before him and say:
"The son of Mao Yigao, Rui Zheng, this year in the north..."
"You are the eighth-ranked candidate for the provincial examination in Jingxiang. You may go now and report this in secret; entrust it to Mao and do not let it leak out.
When the appointed time arrives, the signs will correspond. I shall oversee your sustenance while you live and your funeral and burial after you die.

Moved by your sincere devotion to reciting the sutras despite being childless, I have specifically granted this reward to you as an exhortation to the world. The fifth *zhī* (fungus) was indeed consistent with his ranking in the autumn examination. Thus...
He relinquished his residence to an elderly neighbor and provided for him; he attended to all the latter’s affairs until the end of his life.

As for Wuzhi, he generally did not wish to speak of these matters constantly to others. This is what I heard personally from his younger brother, Daxue Junfang, while I was reading by the Tiexi River.
Pu Kechong, a student of the Xiu-shui Academy, was born blind; his wife, née Wang, had one son and one daughter who both died of smallpox in succession.

He wept for them with excessive grief until both his eyes became blind. Thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, continuing without interruption for several years. One...

While he was reciting the sutras daily, his left eye suddenly began to flow with tears, and the pain was as if it were being cut or torn. Immediately, however, it became clear and bright. After several days, his right eye suffered the same.
Consequently, he became even more devout in his recitations. One night, he dreamed that the Buddha spoke to him, saying:

"You originally had no son; because of your recitation of the sutras, I grant you one. Subsequently, Lady Wang unexpectedly became pregnant again and gave birth to a son, who was thus named Jingci (Sutra-Gifted).
It exists to this day.
The servant of the Fan family from Bongsonggyo-bang, whose name I have forgotten, recited the sutras for me. When I was eight or nine years old, I saw him carrying vegetables on his shoulder.

He carried his goods to the marketplace, muttering prayers incessantly with his lips. Hearing that he rose early to attend to his business, one would find him before the Buddha, burning incense and prostrating;

he would kneel and recite several scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* before departing. In the evening, he would invariably go to the Buddha hall of Jinming Temple to pay homage to the Buddha and dedicate the merit, only then returning home.
On his way back, whenever he encountered living beings, he would always reduce his spending to purchase them for release. Whenever he met beggars, he would give to them.
When there were those who were ill, he would reduce his own food and give it to them as alms. In performing these good deeds, he always maintained a sincere heart and genuine intent.

When the head of the household gave him to his wife, she did not wish for it; consequently, he was permitted to leave the home life. He went to Master Dachen Chan of Santaba to shave his head and become a disciple.
For several years, he wore the monastic robes and labored diligently at manual tasks. All the arduous duties in the meditation hall, he took upon himself entirely, never once complaining.

He grew weary. Suddenly, one day, he manifested illness and addressed the assembly, saying: "In a previous life, I was negligent in my recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Therefore, as punishment, I was made a human slave. Now that my term has ended, I shall go to a good realm to take birth. He then suddenly closed his eyes and passed away. Alas! When ordinary people view others, they distinguish between the honorable and the lowly, assigning them weight accordingly. But when Buddhas and devas view people, they ought to distinguish the honorable from the lowly solely by means of goodness and evil.

As it is said: [The text continues with a verse: "Those who have long practiced the Way, Even if they are currently lowly, Will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood. If one does not practice the Way, Even if one is currently noble, One will surely fall into the three evil realms. Thus, one should know that the Buddha’s eye views all beings with impartiality; there is no distinction between high and low.
